title: Joseph’s rise and the going out from Egypt
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα ὁ Κέλσος ὁσιας ἑνεκεν μετὰ πάσης ἀσαφείας ὑπομιμνήσκεται τῶν ὀνειράτων τοῦ ἀρχισινοχόου καὶ τοῦ ἀρχισιτοποιοῦ καὶ τοῦ Φαραὼ καὶ τῖς λύσεως αὐτῶν ἐξ ἧς προήχθη ἀπὸ τῆς φυλακῆς ἐπὶ τὸ ἐμπιστευθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ Φαραὼ τὸν δεύτερον κατ᾿ Αἰγυπτίων θρόνον ὁ Ἰωσήφ τί οὖν ἄτοπον εἶχεν ὁ λόγος τῆς ἱστορίας καὶ καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸν ὅτι αὐτὰ ἔθηκεν ἐν μέρει κατηγορίας ὁ ἀληθῆ λόγον ἐπγράψας τὸν οὐ δόγματα ἐκτιθέμενον ἀλλὰ Χριστιανῶν καὶ Ἰουδαιων κατηγορήσαντα; καὶ τοῖς πωλήσασί γε ἀδελφοῖς λιμώττουσι καὶ σταλεῖσι κατ᾿ ἐμπορίαν μετὰ τῶν ὄνων φησὶ χαριζόμενον τὸν πραθέντα πεποιηκέναι ἃ οὐδὲ παρέστησεν ὁ Κέλσος, καὶ τὸν ἀναγνωρισμὸν δὲ τίθησιν, οὐκ οἶδα τί βουλόμενος καὶ τί ἐμφαίνων ἄτοπον ἐκ τοῦ ἀναγνωρισμοῦ· οὐδὲ γὰρ, ὡς ἔστιν εἰπεῖν, καὶ αὐτῷ τῷ Μώμῳ δυνατὸν ἦν τούτων εὐλόγως κατηγορεῖν, καὶ χωρὶς τῆς τροπολογίας ἐχόντων πολὺ τὸ ἀγωγόν, τίθησι δὲ καὶ τὸν εἰς δοῦλον πραθέντα Ἰωσὴφ ἐλευθερούμενον καὶ μετὰ πομπῆς ἐπανιόντα πρὸς τὸν τοῦ πατρὸς τάφον καὶ νομίζει κατηγορίαν περιέχειν τὸν λόγον εἰπὼν τό· ὑφ᾿ οὗ (δῆλον δ᾿ ὅτι τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ) τὸ λαμπρὸν καὶ θεσπέσιον Ἰουδαίων γένος, ἐπὶ πλῆθος ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ σπαρὲν, ἔξω που παροικεῖν καὶ ποιμαίνειν ἐν τοῖς ἀτίμοις ἐκελεύσθη, καὶ προσέθηκεν ἀπὸ τῆς μισητικῆς ἑαυτοῦ προαιρέσεως τὸ ἐν ἀτίμοις αὐτοὺς κεκελεῦσθαι ποιμαίνειν, οὐ παραστήσας, πῶς Γεσὲμ ὁ Αἰγυπτίων νομὸς ἄτιμός ἐστι, τὴν δ᾿ ἀπ᾿ Αἰγύπτου ἔξοδον τοῦ λαοῦ φυγὴν ὠνόμασεν, οὐδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν ὑπομνησθεὶς τῶν ἐν τῇ Ἐξόδῳ γεγραμμένων περὶ τῆς ἐξόδου τῶν Ἑβραίων ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου, ἐξεθέμεθα δὲ καὶ ταῦτα, παραδεικνύντες ὅτι καὶ τὰ μηδὲ κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν τοῦ κατηγορεῖσθαι φανέντα ἄξια ἔθηκεν ἐν μοίρᾳ κατηγορίας καὶ φλυαρίας ὁ Κέλσος, μὴ παραστήσας λόγῳ ὃ οἴεται μοχθηρὸν τῆς γραφῆς ἡμῶν.
pass_a_gloss: After these things Celsus, for form's sake (ὁσίας ἕνεκεν), with all unclarity (ἀσαφείας), makes mention (ὑπομιμνήσκεται) of the dreams (ὀνειράτων) of the chief cupbearer (ἀρχισινοχόου) and the chief baker (ἀρχισιτοποιοῦ) and of Pharaoh and of their solution/interpretation (λύσεως), from which Joseph was brought forward (προήχθη) from the prison to being entrusted (ἐμπιστευθῆναι) by Pharaoh with the second throne (θρόνον) over the Egyptians. What then absurd did the account (λόγος) of the history have even in itself (καθ' ἑαυτόν), that he placed these in part of accusation (ἐν μέρει κατηγορίας), he who inscribed (ἐπιγράψας) as True Doctrine/Word (ἀληθῆ λόγον) the (book) setting out not doctrines (δόγματα) but having accused Christians and Jews? And to the brothers who sold (him), starving (λιμώττουσι) and sent (σταλεῖσι) for trade (κατ' ἐμπορίαν) with the asses (ὄνων), he says the one sold (πραθέντα), doing favours (χαριζόμενον), did things which Celsus did not even present (παρέστησεν); and he puts (τίθησιν) the recognition (ἀναγνωρισμόν) too, I do not know wishing what and showing (ἐμφαίνων) what absurd from the recognition; for not even, so to say, to Momus himself was it possible reasonably (εὐλόγως) to accuse these things, which even apart from tropology have much attraction/persuasive pull (ἀγωγόν). He puts also Joseph sold into slavery being freed (ἐλευθερούμενον) and with procession (πομπῆς) returning (ἐπανιόντα) to the tomb (τάφον) of the father, and he thinks the account contains accusation, having said: 'by whom (clearly of Joseph) the splendid (λαμπρόν) and divine/wondrous (θεσπέσιον) race of the Jews, sown/spread (σπαρέν) to a multitude (πλῆθος) in Egypt, was ordered (ἐκελεύσθη) to sojourn (παροικεῖν) somewhere outside and to shepherd (ποιμαίνειν) in the dishonoured (ἀτίμοις) (places)'; and he added from his hating (μισητικῆς) disposition/choice (προαιρέσεως) that they were ordered to shepherd in dishonoured places, not having shown how Goshen (Γεσέμ), the Egyptians' nome/district (νομός), is dishonoured; and the exodus (ἔξοδον) of the people from Egypt he named flight (φυγήν), not even at all (οὐδὲ τὴν ἀρχήν) having recalled the things written in Exodus about the exodus of the Hebrews from the land of Egypt. And we set out these things too, showing that Celsus placed in the portion (μοίρᾳ) of accusation and nonsense (φλυαρίας) even the things not appearing worthy of being accused even according to the letter (κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν), not having established by reason (λόγῳ) what he thinks wicked/faulty (μοχθηρόν) in our scripture.
pass_b_english: After this Celsus, for form’s sake and very obscurely, recalls the dreams of the chief cupbearer and the chief baker and of Pharaoh, and their interpretation (Genesis 40:1–41:36), as a result of which Joseph was brought out of prison and entrusted by Pharaoh with the second throne over the Egyptians (Genesis 41:14; Genesis 41:40–43). What absurdity, then, did the account of the history contain, even taken by itself, that he should set it down as part of his accusation, he who gave the title True Doctrine to a book that sets out no doctrines but accuses Christians and Jews?

He also says that the one who had been sold did things as a favour to the brothers who sold him, when they were starving and had been sent with their donkeys to trade (Genesis 42:1–3; Genesis 42:26), though Celsus does not even make clear what these things were. He sets down the recognition as well (Genesis 45:1–15), with what purpose I do not know, or what absurdity he means to point out in the recognition. For not even Momus himself, so to speak, could reasonably find fault with these things, which even apart from their figurative sense have great appeal.

He also sets down that Joseph, who had been sold as a slave, was set free and returned in procession to his father’s tomb (Genesis 50:7–13), and he thinks the account contains grounds for accusation, saying: “by whom” (that is, plainly, Joseph) “the splendid and godlike race of the Jews, spread abroad in great numbers in Egypt, was ordered to live as aliens somewhere outside and to tend flocks in despised places.” And out of his own hostile disposition he has added that they were ordered to tend flocks in despised places, without showing how Goshen, the district of Egypt, is despised (Genesis 46:34; Genesis 47:6). And he called the departure of the people from Egypt a flight, without so much as recalling what is written in Exodus about the departure of the Hebrews from the land of Egypt (Exodus 12:31–42).

We have set these things out as well, to show that Celsus placed under the heading of accusation and idle talk even things that do not appear, even according to the letter, to deserve accusation, without establishing by argument what he thinks is bad in our Scripture.

ἐπανιόντα: 'went up in procession' changed to 'returned in procession' (the verb means going back); note updated
Celsus's quoted clause (εἰπὼν τό … ἐκελεύσθη) and Origen's aside checked; Genesis 46:34, 47:6 and Exodus 12:31–42 checked; no change

Copy-text: staged source_4.json section 47 (Koetschau 4.47). ὁσίας ἕνεκεν taken in the idiomatic sense ‘for form’s sake’ (LSJ ὁσία: ὁσίας ἕνεκα), not ‘for piety’s sake’; μετὰ πάσης ἀσαφείας as ‘very obscurely’. Staged text has typos (ἐπγράψας for ἐπιγράψας, τῖς for τῆς, ὁσιας for ὁσίας, Ἰουδαιων); read as the obvious forms. ‘True Doctrine’ renders ἀληθῆ λόγον, the title of Celsus’s book; Origen plays on λόγος/δόγματα. The kindness to the brothers and the recognition are Celsus’s items, reported indirectly; only the clause introduced by εἰπὼν τό (‘by whom … in despised places’) is set in quotation marks as Celsus’s words, with Origen’s aside ‘that is, plainly, Joseph’ in parentheses. σπαρέν ἐπὶ πλῆθος rendered ‘spread abroad in great numbers’ (σπείρω, ‘sow, scatter’). Goshen: Joseph tells his family to say they are herdsmen so they may live in Goshen (Genesis 46:34), and Pharaoh gives them ‘the best of the land’ (Genesis 47:6), which is Origen’s implied answer. ‘The second throne’: Genesis 41:40 (‘only in the throne will I be greater than you’) and 41:43 (the second chariot). Momus is the Greek god of fault-finding. ‘Returned in procession to his father’s tomb’ (ἐπανιόντα) follows Celsus’s summary; Genesis 50:7–13 tells of the great company that went up to bury Jacob.
